Akhaltsikhe Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Akhaltsikhe, Georgia

Not demolished. Akhaltsikhe, first mentioned in 12th-century chronicles, endured invasions by Mongols, Iranians, and Turks before Ottoman conquest in 1576 made it a pasha's seat; Russia annexed the city following the 1828-29 war and the Treaty of Adrianople. Jews are first documented there in 1745 by Georgian historian Bakhushti Bagrationi, settling in a district west of the Rabati Fortress; the first synagogue was built in 1740, a second in 1863. Nineteenth-century migration from Abastumani, Akhaldaba, and Dviri boosted the community, mostly active in international trade with Persia, Turkey, and Russia. Population grew from 117 families in 1830 to 1,738 by 1897 and 3,627 by 1915; Akhaltsikhe Jews later built Tbilisi's well-known 'Akhaltsikhe Synagogue' and maintained 17 markets, collective farms, a kindergarten, school, library, and a charity for poor peasants there. The community sharply declined in the 1970s; today only one Jewish resident, Simon Levishvili, remains, still caring for the synagogue and cemetery. The Great Synagogue (built 1863, renovated 2012) remains a national heritage site, though it now lacks a regular minyan; a second synagogue (1905) closed in 1952 and has since served variously as a cinema, library, culture house, billiard room, and gym before falling into disuse. Akhaltsikhe was also home to Shalom Koboshvili (1876-1941), Georgia's first Jewish painter, who only began painting at 61 while working as a museum guard, producing a three-year documentary chronicle of Georgian Jewish daily life before his death. This cemetery, on a hill overlooking the historic Jewish quarter and enclosed by a high stone fence, holds graves possibly dating to the 17th century; an 1863 account described epitaphs from 1810 and the synagogue from 1741, while researcher Nisan Babalikashvili argued in 1971 for tombstones as early as 1756 or 1765. Some inscriptions in Ladino suggest at least some community members traced Ottoman and ultimately Iberian Peninsula origins.
